rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec quarter-point hike fully priced, from ~89% Friday; Jan ~67% (Reuters); CME FedWatch ~96% (Hercules); ECB Dec ~90%; BoE Dec ~84% (from ~80%); BoJ Dec ~84%; BoC Dec ~44%
rows.read: Traders now fully expect a quarter-point Fed hike in December and see a good chance of another in January. The Bank of England sounds firmer too, and the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan are expected to hike in December. The Fed still looks set to go furthest, which keeps the dollar on top.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US composite PMI Nov 54.6 (Oct 55.9), services 54.7 vs 55.6 fcst, mfg 54.5 in line; Germany composite 55.0; France 46.2; euro area 51.7; UK 52.3, services 52.0; Chicago Fed activity index Oct −0.06
rows.read: Business surveys showed the US economy and UK services slowing in November, while Germany sped up and France shrank. None of it changed what central banks are expected to do, so growth news is taking a back seat to interest rates for now.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: US core PCE Oct due Wed (fcst +0.3% m/m, 3.2% y/y); Williams: inflation about 3.5%; UK CPI Oct 3.6%; euro-area CPI Oct 4.0%; Australia CPI Oct due Tue 6:30 PM CT (fcst 4.8% y/y)
rows.read: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. New York Fed President John Williams called US inflation simply too high. US core inflation on Wednesday and Australian inflation on Tuesday evening are the week's big tests.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.read: US stocks jumped after Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang as chief executive, ending last week's selloff. Calmer markets drew money out of the yen and the franc. With fear gone, the dollar rose on interest rates instead.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent ~$89.25 (−3.6%), low ~$89.07, lowest since Sep 4; WTI ~$80.29 (−3.6%); gold ~$3,645 (+3.4% from Friday)
rows.read: Oil fell below $90 as more Middle East supply reached the market, which hurts the Canadian dollar and helps oil importers like the euro area and Japan. Gold won back much of last week's fall, which gives the Aussie some support.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: Hedge funds (CFTC, Nov 17): USD index −1.3K (flipped short), EUR −76.6K, GBP +28.8K, JPY −23.8K, CHF −19.8K, CAD −72.1K, AUD +38.0K, NZD −23.6K; asset managers GBP −104.6K, AUD −182.7K, EUR +147.2K
rows.read: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: US 10-year near 5% (Hercules); France composite PMI 46.2, a six-month low; ECB Financial Stability Review: France debt 119% of GDP, deficit 5.5%
rows.read: France's debts weigh more now that its economy looks close to recession. Heavy US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs near 5%, which supports the dollar's yield but raises questions about debt over time.
